meta.title: Who really said "Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Einstein's words. Composer Roger Sessions paraphrased him 'in effect' in the New York Times in 1950; Louis Zukofsky put the same line in quotation marks months later, and the paraphrase hardened into a quotation. Einstein's real 1933 sentence is far longer.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler'?
meta.ogDescription: A 1950 paraphrase by composer Roger Sessions — who flagged it as 'in effect' — later printed as a direct Einstein quotation. Einstein's actual 1933 wording is much longer.

answer.label: Not Einstein's wording — a 1950 paraphrase by Roger Sessions
answer.sourceLine: Writing in The New York Times on 8 January 1950, the composer Roger Sessions said Einstein had remarked “in effect, that everything should be as simple as it can be but not simpler.” The words ‘in effect’ mark it plainly as a paraphrase. Five months later Louis Zukofsky printed the same line inside quotation marks and credited it straight to Einstein — and that is the version the world kept.

source.heading: What Einstein actually said

docMeta.dd: Roger Sessions, The New York Times, 8 January 1950

source.excerpt: It can scarcely be denied that the supreme goal of all theory is to make the irreducible basic elements as simple and as few as possible without having to surrender the adequate representation of a single datum of experience.
trail: Roger Sessions, ‘How a “Difficult” Composer Gets That Way,’ The New York Times, 8 January 1950 — reports that Einstein said ‘in effect, that everything should be as simple as it can be but not simpler.’ The hedge is in the original Quote Investigator ↗.

Louis Zukofsky, reviewing in Poetry (June 1950), printed ‘Everything should be as simple as it can be, but not simpler’ in quotation marks, credited directly to Einstein — the moment a paraphrase became a quotation full trace ↗.

Einstein’s own statement of the idea, from his Herbert Spencer Lecture at Oxford on 10 June 1933, runs to thirty-eight words and never uses the aphorism’s snap. Wikiquote lists the short form only as attributed sourced vs attributed ↗.
source.excerptNote: Einstein’s actual sentence from the 1933 Herbert Spencer Lecture. Same idea — nothing like the aphorism’s compactness, which is Sessions’ contribution, not his.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Einstein
author.bio: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) really did argue for theoretical economy — that a theory should reduce to the fewest irreducible elements that still account for the evidence. That makes this aphorism unusually plausible: it is a fair compression of a view he genuinely held, which is precisely why it survived unchallenged for seventy years. The idea is his; the sentence is a composer’s.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This one is unusually well documented, because the paraphrase and its conversion into a quotation happened five months apart in print, and both are dated.

items.why: Sessions wrote that Einstein said it ‘in effect’ — an explicit signal that he was summarising, not quoting. That qualifier was dropped by everyone who repeated it trace ↗.
Months later Zukofsky printed the sentence in quotation marks and credited Einstein directly. Once a paraphrase acquires quotation marks in print, it is effectively impossible to reel back in.

His actual formulation is a thirty-eight-word sentence about making basic elements ‘as simple and as few as possible’ without surrendering the representation of experience — the same thought, none of the same words sourced text ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is genuinely Einstein’s; the sentence is Roger Sessions’ 1950 paraphrase, promoted to a quotation by Louis Zukofsky the same year full trace ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is a better sentence than the one Einstein wrote — which is exactly why it won. The ‘but not simpler’ turn does real work: it guards against the lazy reading that simplicity alone is the goal, and it does so in four words.
That is also the trap. A paraphrase that improves on the original is the hardest kind to dislodge, because everyone who repeats it feels they are being faithful to the thought.
detailsBody: Einstein, Oxford 1933: ‘…to make the irreducible basic elements as simple and as few as possible without having to surrender the adequate representation of a single datum of experience.’
Sessions, NYT, 8 Jan 1950: Einstein said ‘in effect, that everything should be as simple as it can be but not simpler.’
Zukofsky, Poetry, June 1950: ‘Everything should be as simple as it can be, but not simpler’ — in quotation marks, credited to Einstein.
Modern form: ‘Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler.’
context.pull: Sessions wrote that Einstein said it "in effect." Everyone since has dropped the hedge.
